Airbnb Pricing, Location and Listing Characteristics Investigation¶

AnalystLab Africa Experience Lab · Week 1 · Track B (Data Science) Intern: Nelson Nyamweya

This notebook is the reproducible analysis behind the Track B statistical report. Run it top to bottom (Kernel → Restart & Run All). It reads the four supplied files from data/raw/ and writes every table to outputs/tables/ and every figure to outputs/figures/.

0. Business problem and research design¶

Business problem. Stakeholders evaluating ten Airbnb markets need to know which listing characteristics go with higher advertised prices in each market, how hosts differ between markets, and whether review activity says anything about listing ratings. Raw listing counts and average prices cannot answer this: prices are in ten different currencies, contain extreme values, and many fields are missing.

Why it matters. Hosts, property investors and market analysts use advertised-price benchmarks to position listings and compare markets. Getting the drivers wrong (for example, comparing 100 THB with 100 EUR, or reading a review count as satisfaction) leads to poor pricing and investment decisions.

Intended users. Market analysts, host-support and partnerships teams, and property investors who need evidence-based, city-specific benchmarks.

Decisions supported. City-specific price benchmarking by room type and capacity; deciding which listing attributes to collect or emphasise; prioritising host-responsiveness programmes by city; deciding whether review volume can be used as a quality proxy.

Primary research problem¶

Which listing characteristics (room type, accommodation capacity and number of bedrooms) are associated with higher advertised prices within each of the 10 cities, measured in each city's local currency?

Supporting research questions¶

  • RQ1. Do advertised prices differ across room types within each city?
  • RQ2. Are accommodation capacity and number of bedrooms associated with advertised price within each city?
  • RQ3. Is review activity (number of review records) associated with the listing-level overall review rating?
  • RQ4. Do host response indicators (response rate, Superhost status) differ across cities?

Variables required. price, city, room_type, property_type, accommodates, bedrooms (Listings); review_scores_rating (Listings); host_response_rate, host_response_time, host_is_superhost (Listings); listing_id, review_id, date (Reviews).

Expected analytical outcome. City-by-city effect sizes (not just p-values) showing how much room type and capacity move the median advertised price; a measured relationship between review volume and rating; a city comparison of host responsiveness.

Limitations of the evidence (summary). Prices are advertised nightly prices in local currency, not revenue or occupancy. The Reviews file holds dates and IDs only, no review text or per-review ratings. District is only populated for New York. Results are associations in an observational snapshot (reviews up to 1 March 2021), not causal effects. Full discussion in Section 7.

Success criteria (Track B)¶

  1. Reconciliation: record counts reproduce the brief exactly (279,712 listings × 33 columns; 5,373,143 reviews × 4 columns; 160 duplicated review_id values; 0 orphan reviews). Checked by assert statements below.
  2. Currency-safe analysis: no statistical test pools raw prices across cities; every price result is reported per city in its local currency (or as a currency-free ratio to the city median).
  3. Hypothesis coverage: at least three hypotheses tested, each with H0/H1, test choice, assumptions, effect size and multiple-testing correction (Holm), plus a robustness re-run on 1st–99th percentile trimmed prices.
  4. Visual evidence: at least five publication-quality figures saved to outputs/figures/.
  5. Reproducibility: a clean Restart & Run All regenerates every table and figure without manual steps.

Finding. Each of the 160 repeated IDs appears exactly twice, with the same date and same reviewer but on two different listings. All 22 listings involved are in Rome, belong to just 2 hosts, and form 11 pairs: an older listing (e.g. 5878807) and a newer one with an ID in the 22,219,0xx–22,219,2xx range. The most plausible explanation is that reviews were carried over when properties were re-listed or migrated under a new listing; it is not a loading error (no row is fully identical).

Treatment (documented, not deleted automatically).

  • All 5,373,143 rows are kept. (listing_id, review_id) is used as the composite key.
  • For listing-level review counts each listing keeps its own records, because that is what each listing displays.
  • For market-level totals (city/time series of unique review events) the duplicate is counted once: 5,373,143 − 160 = 5,372,983 unique review events. The difference is 0.003% of rows, so it cannot change any conclusion, but both figures are reported.

Observations. 113 listings advertise a price of 0 or less (invalid for a nightly price). Every city has a long right tail: the maximum is between ~100× and ~2,200× the city median (e.g. Rio de Janeiro max 625,216 BRL vs median 280 BRL), which is typical of placeholder or mis-keyed prices. Medians range from 65 (Rome, EUR) to 1,100 (Bangkok, THB) purely because of currency, which is why raw prices are never pooled across cities.

Interpretation. district is 86.8% missing because it is only populated for New York, so district analysis is restricted to New York and neighbourhood (complete) is used elsewhere. Host response/acceptance fields are 40–46% missing and missingness varies strongly by city, so it is not random: treating it as a separate "not reported" category is safer than imputing. review_scores_rating is missing for 32.7% of listings, mostly listings with no reviews. bedrooms (10.5% missing) is mostly missing for studios and shared/hotel rooms.

3. Cleaning and transformation decisions¶

In [10]:
L = listings_raw.copy()
log = []
def step(desc, before, after): log.append({"step": desc, "rows_before": before, "rows_after": after, "rows_removed": before - after})

for c in ["host_is_superhost", "host_has_profile_pic", "host_identity_verified", "instant_bookable"]:
    L[c] = L[c].map({"t": True, "f": False})
L["host_since"] = pd.to_datetime(L.host_since, errors="coerce")
L["currency"] = L.city.map(CURRENCY)
L["amenities_count"] = L.amenities.str.count('",') + L.amenities.str.contains('"').astype(int)
L["host_response_time"] = L.host_response_time.fillna("not reported")

n0 = len(L); L = L[L.price > 0]; step("Remove non-positive prices (price <= 0)", n0, len(L))
n0 = len(L); L = L[L.accommodates > 0]; step("Remove accommodates = 0 (invalid capacity)", n0, len(L))

# Extreme prices are KEPT for the main (rank-based) tests and flagged; a trimmed copy is used for robustness checks.
q = L.groupby("city").price.quantile([.01, .99]).unstack()
L["price_extreme_flag"] = (L.price < L.city.map(q[0.01])) | (L.price > L.city.map(q[0.99]))
L["log_price"] = np.log(L.price)
L["price_rel_city_median"] = L.price / L.groupby("city").price.transform("median")  # currency-free index
L["accommodates_grp"] = pd.cut(L.accommodates, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 16], labels=["1", "2", "3", "4", "5-6", "7-8", "9+"])
L["bedrooms_grp"] = pd.cut(L.bedrooms, [0, 1, 2, 3, 50], labels=["1", "2", "3", "4+"])

# Review aggregates (listing level: own records; market level: unique review events)
R = reviews_raw.copy(); R["date"] = pd.to_datetime(R.date)
rev_per_listing = R.groupby("listing_id").agg(review_count=("review_id", "size"),
                                              first_review=("date", "min"), last_review=("date", "max"))
L = L.merge(rev_per_listing, left_on="listing_id", right_index=True, how="left")
L["review_count"] = L.review_count.fillna(0).astype(int)
L["reviews_last_12m"] = L.listing_id.map(R[R.date > "2020-03-01"].groupby("listing_id").size()).fillna(0).astype(int)

R_unique = R.drop_duplicates("review_id").merge(listings_raw[["listing_id", "city"]], on="listing_id")
print("Unique review events:", len(R_unique))
assert len(R_unique) == 5373143 - 160

cleaning_log = pd.DataFrame(log); cleaning_log.to_csv(TAB / "T06_cleaning_log.csv", index=False)
print("Rows flagged as extreme (outside city 1st–99th pct):", int(L.price_extreme_flag.sum()))
L.drop(columns=["name", "amenities", "host_location"]).to_parquet(PROC / "listings_clean.parquet", index=False)
cleaning_log

Unique review events: 5372983
Rows flagged as extreme (outside city 1st–99th pct): 5094
Out[10]:
step rows_before rows_after rows_removed
0 Remove non-positive prices (price <= 0) 279712 279599 113
1 Remove accommodates = 0 (invalid capacity) 279599 279599 0
Decision Why
Drop 113 rows with price ≤ 0 A nightly advertised price of 0 or less is invalid.
Drop rows with accommodates = 0 Capacity of zero guests is invalid. All 85 such rows also had price ≤ 0, so this step removes no further rows (113 removed in total).
Keep extreme prices, flag those outside each city's 1st–99th percentile Deleting them would be arbitrary; rank-based tests are robust to them, and every test is re-run on the trimmed data as a sensitivity check.
Analyse prices within city, plus a currency-free price / city median index No currency field; pooling raw amounts would compare different currencies. No exchange-rate conversion was needed because no test pools cities.
host_response_time missing → "not reported" Missingness is city-dependent (not random); imputation would invent behaviour.
Rates, ratings and bedrooms left as missing; tests use complete cases for the variables involved Avoids fabricating values; sample sizes reported per test.
Review counts from Reviews.csv per listing; market totals de-duplicate review_id See Section 2.2.
Listing names, host location, host/reviewer IDs not used in outputs Privacy: not needed for the research questions.

    sns.histplot(d.price, bins=50, log_scale=True, ax=ax, color="#4C72B0")

    ax.set(title=f"{city} ({CURRENCY[city]})\nmedian {med:,.0f}", xlabel=f"Price ({CURRENCY[city]}, log scale)", ylabel="")
    ax.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(mticker.NullFormatter()); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:,.0f}"))
fig.suptitle("Distribution of advertised nightly price within each city, local currency (1st–99th pct)", y=1.02, fontsize=14)
fig.tight_layout(); save(fig, "F03_price_distribution_by_city")

Within every city the price distribution is strongly right-skewed and roughly log-normal. This justifies (a) medians rather than means, (b) rank-based tests, and (c) log price in regression.

In every city the median price rises steadily with capacity: single-guest listings advertise roughly 0.4–0.6× the city median, while listings for 7–8 guests advertise roughly 1.8–4.2× it. 5. Hypothesis tests¶

General approach:

  • Prices are never pooled across currencies. Price tests run separately in each city.
  • Prices are skewed with extreme values, so the main tests are rank-based (Kruskal–Wallis, Mann–Whitney U, Spearman). These assume independent observations and, for location interpretation, similarly shaped distributions; they make no normality assumption.
  • With n in the thousands, almost any difference is "significant", so each test reports an effect size: ε² for Kruskal–Wallis (0.01 small, 0.08 medium, 0.26 large), rank-biserial r for Mann–Whitney, ρ for Spearman (0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large).
  • p-values are adjusted with Holm's method across the 10 cities within each hypothesis (α = 0.05).
  • Robustness: each price test is re-run excluding prices outside the city 1st–99th percentile.
In [23]:
def eps2_kw(H, n, k): return max((H - k + 1) / (n - k), 0)
def holm(p): return multipletests(p, method="holm")[1]
def mag_eps(e): return "large" if e >= .26 else "medium" if e >= .08 else "small" if e >= .01 else "negligible"
def mag_rho(r): r = abs(r); return "large" if r >= .5 else "medium" if r >= .3 else "small" if r >= .1 else "negligible"

H1 — Advertised prices differ across room types within each city (RQ1)¶

  • H0: Within a city, the price distributions of the room types are identical.
  • H1: At least one room type has a different price distribution.
  • Variables: price (local currency, outcome), room_type (4 groups).
  • Test: Kruskal–Wallis H per city; post-hoc Mann–Whitney U Entire place vs Private room with rank-biserial r. Chosen because prices are non-normal with heavy tails and group variances differ (Levene test below).
In [24]:
def h1(df):
    rows = []
    for city in city_order:
        d = df[df.city == city]
        groups = [g.price.values for _, g in d.groupby("room_type") if len(g) >= 20]
        H, p = stats.kruskal(*groups)
        lev_p = stats.levene(*[np.log(g) for g in groups]).pvalue
        e, pr = d[d.room_type == "Entire place"].price, d[d.room_type == "Private room"].price
        U, p_mw = stats.mannwhitneyu(e, pr, alternative="two-sided")
        rows.append({"city": city, "currency": CURRENCY[city], "n": len(d), "groups": len(groups), "H": H, "p": p,
                     "epsilon2": eps2_kw(H, len(d), len(groups)), "levene_p_logprice": lev_p,
                     "median_entire": e.median(), "median_private": pr.median(),
                     "entire_to_private_ratio": e.median() / pr.median(),
                     "rank_biserial_entire_vs_private": 1 - 2 * U / (len(e) * len(pr)), "p_mw": p_mw})
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    out["p_holm"], out["p_mw_holm"] = holm(out.p), holm(out.p_mw)
    out["effect"] = out.epsilon2.map(mag_eps)
    return out

H1 = h1(L); H1_trim = h1(L[~L.price_extreme_flag])

H1_trim.round(4).to_csv(TAB / "T14b_H1_room_type_price_trimmed.csv", index=False)

Robustness (trimmed 1-99%): epsilon2 range 0.04 - 0.426 | all Holm p < 0.05: True

Interpretation. H0 is rejected in all 10 cities (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). The effect size varies a lot between markets: large in Sydney, New York, Mexico City and Hong Kong (ε² 0.27–0.43), medium in Istanbul, Rome, Rio de Janeiro, Cape Town and Paris (ε² 0.08–0.22), and only small in Bangkok (ε² 0.05). An entire place advertises at about 1.5–2.6× the median price of a private room in the same city (e.g. Sydney 176 vs 68 AUD; New York 140 vs 60 USD; Paris 82 vs 53 EUR), except Bangkok (1,192 vs 1,000 THB, 1.2×). Paris has a smaller effect partly because 86% of its listings are entire places, mostly small apartments. Levene's test shows unequal variances, which supports the choice of rank-based tests. Results are essentially unchanged after trimming extreme prices. Practical meaning: any price benchmark that does not separate room types is misleading.

H2 — Accommodation capacity and bedrooms are positively associated with price within each city (RQ2)¶

  • H0: ρ(capacity, price) = 0 within a city. H1: ρ > 0 (one-sided, a positive association is expected).
  • Variables: accommodates, bedrooms, price (local currency).
  • Test: Spearman rank correlation per city (monotonic, robust to outliers). Assumes independent observations and a monotonic relationship.
  • Supplementary model: OLS of log(price) on accommodates, bedrooms and room_type per city with HC3 robust standard errors, to see whether capacity still matters once room type is held constant. Coefficients are converted to % change in price per extra guest.
In [26]:
def h2(df):
    rows = []
    for city in city_order:
        d = df[df.city == city]
        r_a, p_a = stats.spearmanr(d.accommodates, d.price, alternative="greater")
        db = d.dropna(subset=["bedrooms"])
        r_b, p_b = stats.spearmanr(db.bedrooms, db.price, alternative="greater")
        m = smf.ols("log_price ~ accommodates + bedrooms + C(room_type, Treatment('Entire place'))", data=db).fit(cov_type="HC3")
        rows.append({"city": city, "currency": CURRENCY[city], "n": len(d), "rho_accommodates": r_a, "p_acc": p_a,
                     "n_bedrooms": len(db), "rho_bedrooms": r_b, "p_bed": p_b,
                     "ols_pct_per_extra_guest": (np.exp(m.params["accommodates"]) - 1) * 100,
                     "ols_pct_per_extra_bedroom": (np.exp(m.params["bedrooms"]) - 1) * 100,
                     "ols_p_accommodates": m.pvalues["accommodates"], "ols_r2": m.rsquared})
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    out["p_acc_holm"], out["p_bed_holm"] = holm(out.p_acc), holm(out.p_bed)
    out["effect_acc"] = out.rho_accommodates.map(mag_rho)
    return out

H2 = h2(L); H2_trim = h2(L[~L.price_extreme_flag])

Interpretation. H0 is rejected in all 10 cities. Capacity has a medium-to-large positive association with price (ρ = 0.31 in Bangkok up to 0.68 in Sydney and 0.67 in Cape Town) and bedrooms a similar one (ρ 0.37–0.67). Holding room type and bedrooms constant, each additional guest of capacity is associated with roughly a 7–23% higher advertised price (smallest in Rio de Janeiro, largest in Cape Town and Paris). Model R² (0.19 in Bangkok to 0.57 in Sydney) shows these three characteristics explain a substantial but incomplete share of price variation; location, amenities, quality and seasonality are missing. Residual diagnostics show heavy tails, hence the HC3 robust errors. Bedrooms and capacity are correlated (multicollinearity), so their separate coefficients should not be over-interpreted.

H3 — Review activity is associated with the listing's overall rating (RQ3)¶

  • H0: ρ(review_count, review_scores_rating) = 0. H1: ρ ≠ 0 (two-sided).
  • Variables: review_count (from Reviews.csv), review_scores_rating (Listings, 0–100). No currency involved.
  • Test: Spearman correlation, pooled and per city, on listings with a rating. A Kruskal–Wallis test compares ratings across review-volume bands (1–4, 5–19, 20–49, 50–99, 100+ reviews).
  • Assumptions: independent listings; monotonic relationship. Ratings are bounded and ceilinged, which suits a rank test.
In [28]:
rated = L.dropna(subset=["review_scores_rating"]).query("review_count > 0").copy()
rated["volume_band"] = pd.cut(rated.review_count, [0, 4, 19, 49, 99, 10_000], labels=["1-4", "5-19", "20-49", "50-99", "100+"])
rows = []
for city in ["All cities"] + city_order:
    d = rated if city == "All cities" else rated[rated.city == city]
    r, p = stats.spearmanr(d.review_count, d.review_scores_rating)
    rows.append({"city": city, "n": len(d), "rho": r, "p": p})
H3 = pd.DataFrame(rows); H3["p_holm"] = np.r_[H3.p.iloc[0], holm(H3.p.iloc[1:])]; H3["effect"] = H3.rho.map(mag_rho)
band = rated.groupby("volume_band", observed=True).review_scores_rating.agg(["size", "median", "mean", "std",
                                                                              lambda s: (s < 80).mean()*100])
band.columns = ["n", "median", "mean", "sd", "pct_below_80"]
Hk, pk = stats.kruskal(*[g.review_scores_rating for _, g in rated.groupby("volume_band", observed=True)])
print(f"Kruskal-Wallis across volume bands: H = {Hk:,.0f}, p = {pk:.2e}, epsilon2 = {eps2_kw(Hk, len(rated), 5):.3f}")
H3.round(4).to_csv(TAB / "T16_H3_reviews_vs_rating.csv", index=False); band.round(2).to_csv(TAB / "T16b_rating_by_review_volume.csv")

Interpretation. The pooled correlation is statistically significant, small and negative (ρ = −0.20); it is small and negative in nine cities and negligible in Hong Kong (ρ = −0.03). The negative sign does not mean busier listings are worse. It comes from the spread: listings with 1–4 reviews have a median rating of 100 but also the most low scores (SD 15.1; 9.4% rated below 80), while listings with 50+ reviews cluster tightly around 95–96 (SD ≈ 3.7; under 0.1% below 80). This is consistent with a small-sample effect (a rating built from 2 reviews is noisy) and possibly survivorship (poorly rated listings stop attracting stays). Practical meaning: review volume is not a reliable proxy for quality, and ratings based on few reviews should be shown with caution. Review counts measure activity, not satisfaction.

H4 — Host responsiveness differs across cities (RQ4)¶

  • H4a. H0: host response-rate distributions are identical across the 10 cities. H1: at least one city differs. Test: Kruskal–Wallis (response rate is bounded, mostly 100%, highly skewed).
  • H4b. H0: Superhost status is independent of city. H1: it depends on city. Test: χ² test of independence with Cramér's V (assumes expected counts ≥ 5, satisfied).
  • Unit is the listing; hosts with several listings appear more than once, so a host-level re-run is included (one row per host).
In [29]:
rr = L.dropna(subset=["host_response_rate"])
Hr, pr = stats.kruskal(*[g.host_response_rate for _, g in rr.groupby("city")])
hosts = rr.drop_duplicates("host_id")
Hh, ph = stats.kruskal(*[g.host_response_rate for _, g in hosts.groupby("city")])
sh = L.dropna(subset=["host_is_superhost"])
ct = pd.crosstab(sh.city, sh.host_is_superhost)
chi2, pc, dof, exp = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
cramer = np.sqrt(chi2 / (ct.values.sum() * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))
H4 = pd.DataFrame([
    {"test": "H4a Kruskal-Wallis response rate ~ city (listing level)", "n": len(rr), "stat": Hr, "p": pr, "effect": eps2_kw(Hr, len(rr), 10), "effect_name": "epsilon2"},

    {"test": "H4b Chi-square superhost x city", "n": int(ct.values.sum()), "stat": chi2, "p": pc, "effect": cramer, "effect_name": "Cramer's V"},
])

Interpretation. Both nulls are rejected (p < 0.001), but the effect sizes are small (ε² = 0.013 listing level, 0.017 host level; Cramér's V = 0.16). Hosts who report a response rate are highly responsive in every city (median 100%). The bigger difference between cities is whether hosts report response information at all (36% of listings in Paris vs 84% in Hong Kong), and Superhost share ranges from 12% of listings (Sydney, Paris) to 32% (Mexico City). The host-level re-run gives the same conclusion, so multi-listing hosts do not drive the result.

7. Limitations¶

  • Missing listing attributes. Bedrooms (10.5%), ratings (32.7%) and host response/acceptance (40–46%) are missing, and missingness differs by city and room type, so complete-case results describe listings that report these fields, which may be more professional or more active hosts.
  • Currency differences. Raw prices are in 8 currencies. All tests are within city; cross-city comparisons use the ratio to the city median. Absolute cross-city price levels were deliberately not compared; doing so would require dated exchange rates (and ideally purchasing-power adjustment).
  • Unequal listing counts across cities. Paris has ~9× the listings of Hong Kong. Tests are per city, effect sizes are reported, and Holm correction is applied, but small-city estimates are less precise.
  • Duplicate review identifiers. 160 IDs shared by 11 Rome listing pairs. Kept at listing level and de-duplicated at market level; the impact (0.003% of rows) is negligible.
  • Different levels of review activity. 30.8% of listings have no reviews, and the top 10% of listings hold 64% of all review records. Ratings built on few reviews are noisy (H3), and new listings are under-represented in rated subsets.
  • Missing district information. District only exists for New York; neighbourhood is used elsewhere, and its granularity differs by city.
  • Potentially influential extreme prices. Placeholder or mis-keyed prices up to ~2,000× the city median exist. Rank tests limit their influence and trimmed re-runs give the same conclusions.
  • No booking or occupancy records. Prices are advertised and may differ from prices actually paid; review activity is not occupancy, and ratings are not sentiment. Nothing here measures revenue or profitability.
  • Association, not causation. All findings are associations in a cross-sectional snapshot. For example, larger listings advertise higher prices, but this study cannot show that adding capacity causes a higher achievable price; location, quality and amenities are confounders.
  • Timing. Listings were scraped around early 2021, during COVID-19 disruption; patterns may not reflect normal market conditions.

8. Findings and recommendations¶

Key findings

  1. Paris (64.6k), New York (37.0k) and Sydney (33.6k) have the most listings; Hong Kong (7.1k) the fewest. Entire places make up 65% of all listings, private rooms 31%; "Entire apartment" is the most common property type.
  2. Room type separates prices in every city: entire places advertise 1.5–2.6× the median private-room price in the same currency (effect large in 4 cities, medium in 5, small in Bangkok).
  3. Capacity and bedrooms have medium-to-large positive associations with price in every city (ρ 0.31–0.68); each extra guest is associated with roughly 7–23% higher advertised price even after controlling for room type and bedrooms.
  4. Review activity is heavily concentrated: 30.8% of listings have no reviews while the top 10% hold 64% of all review records. Activity peaked in 2019 and collapsed after March 2020.
  5. Review volume is weakly and negatively related to rating (ρ = −0.20) because low-volume listings have far more variable ratings (more perfect 100s and more low scores); ratings stabilise around 95–96 after ~20 reviews.
  6. Host responsiveness differs between cities, but only slightly (small effects); the larger gaps are in how many hosts report response data (36–84%) and in Superhost share (12–32%).

Recommendations

# Action Evidence How to evaluate usefulness
R1 Build price benchmarks per city, per room type, per capacity band, in local currency; never quote one cross-city average. H1 (ε² up to 0.43) and H2 (ρ 0.31–0.68); currency profile (T04). Compare benchmark error (median absolute deviation of listing price from its benchmark cell) against a city-only median; the segmented benchmark should cut error substantially.
R2 Display ratings with a minimum review threshold (e.g. ≥ 10 reviews) or a confidence band, and stop using review count as a quality signal. H3: rating SD falls from 15.1 (1–4 reviews) to 3.6 (100+ reviews) (T16b). Track whether listings flagged as "few reviews" later move toward the mean rating; A/B test whether guests trust thresholded ratings more.
R3 Target host-support campaigns at cities with the lowest response-reporting and Superhost shares, and collect response data consistently. H4; host indicators table (T12). Monitor the reporting share and Superhost share per city quarter on quarter after the campaign.
R4 Collect the data needed for stronger conclusions: currency field, actual booked prices/occupancy, and review text. Limitations, Section 7. Re-run this notebook with the new fields; check whether model R² and decision usefulness improve.
